utterances.text: Well, let's look at item 3 first, and then we'll go back to item 2, and especially the third sentence. Could you please explain the whole of item 3, in fact.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Item 3 explains in greater detail the idea that guided me when I issued this task. To accommodate and protect the civilian population in inhabited places in line with my previous orders. That's why particular units were evacuated or moved out. I am requiring from the subordinate commanders that the civilian population not be out in the open, but that it be accommodated in buildings, inside inhabited places, and that any criminal activity against the civilian population be prevented.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: We see that you said something in brackets, to prevent what?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if someone should perhaps prohibit the civilian population from returning to their homes --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Could you comment on item 2 and then on item 5 after that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before moving on to that, if you would go back, please, to paragraph -- section number 1 which talks of removing all military territorial units from inhabited places. It goes on to say: "And occupy facilities for the purpose of the blockade." What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the military territorial units had to take dominant facilities to block them from attacks by terrorist forces; that's combat control of the territory. So from those facilities they should protect their own forces and all the other forces in the general area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What is the blockade you're talking about there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is a blockade of approach of possibilities for terrorist forces to approach and to suddenly attack these significant features and facilities. As I said, by setting up sentinels and employing the entire system of combat control of the territory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you give me an example of such facilities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with all due respect, allow me to say that the most serious form, the most difficult form, of anti-terrorist combat anywhere in the world is combat control of the territory, protection of the general area of various features and facilities. There are experiences all over the world where suicide bombers penetrate to such facilities or features. So approach should be blocked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I just want you to tell me the nature of the facilities you had in mind. Can you give me an example of such a facility?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, a very specific example, Your Honour, would be the following: The military territorial Podujevo Detachment, which according to its purpose would be deployed in an inhabited place, in a town, securing important buildings, I ordered that it be removed several kilometres further away where there is a major waterworks important for water-supply to the entire area and to block and protect that waterworks from terrorist attacks. They succeeded in this, but the waterworks were hit by NATO's air-strikes and the population was left without water.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, you have explained item 3. Please look at items 2 and 5.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a document of the 23rd of April, and here I order the commanders on -- after having carried out the resubordination of the MUP units, the main forces of the police should be engaged primarily as a priority task on the combat control of the territory and an assessment for such engagement should be carried out at the brigade level.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Well, let's pause here. We'll come to some documents, but to clarify things here you stress the date here. This was after the order by the supreme commander, the Chief of the General Staff, and then the commander of the 3rd Army were issued. And you set a deadline by the 25th, just so that Their Honours can have a clear reference and then we'll come to those documents. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, please look at item 5 on page 2, so it's also on page 2 in the English version, item 5. Can you explain what it means?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In item 5, I prohibited my subordinate commanders from issuing any kind of order having to do with the functioning of civilian organs of authority or the so-called Crisis Staffs, and the unification or coordination and combination of means of defence should be regulated by special orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Please look at item 9.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Item 9, first of all, points to the continuation of previous orders, numerous previous orders, and says: "Continue using all measures to prevent any attempted crime in the areas of responsibility, and should there be any perpetrators of crimes, employ the most serious measures of responsibility." Also, "strengthen measures to ensure order in the units, overall order, in order to preserve the reputation of the members of the Army of Yugoslavia."

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: The last page, item 13, it seems that you stressed here that this order of an ongoing, permanent, character and that the entire corps must be familiarised with it. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, what you said is correct. It's a permanent order, not just because I myself composed it in the midst of wartime chaos, but also because I was convinced at the time that this order provided for important measures. And that's why I required that I be informed regularly through daily combat reports, and this happened throughout the war and this order was always referred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt, Your Honour. The English translation says item 12 is one sentence illegible. I don't know if since the General's here he might be able to tell us what it says.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Could you read item 12, if you can, Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If the usher could zoom in because I see what you all see. I will try. I might be able to recognise something. Oh, yes, yes. "By all means, to the maximum extent, intensify measures of engineer protection, engineer support." So it says: "To the maximum extent, with all available means, take measures of engineering support." I can explain what this means. It means securing manoeuvres, removing land-mines from roads, and especially creating obstacles at the state border to prevent attacks from Albania and Macedonia. So that is to protect the manpower.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Bakrac --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- From attacks, from attacks from the air-space.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, you read an order here concerning your prohibition, or rather, where you prohibited your commanders from interfering in the work of civilian authorities. Can you explain what this means and what this refers to?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was a preventive measure. I must confess that at the time I didn't know that anyone on the territory of Kosovo and Metohija issued any erroneous orders to this effect, but I clearly ordered the commanders, saying them -- telling them that they had absolutely no authority over the civilian government and the civilian authorities in the areas where the army units were deployed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, let us look at 3D592, Exhibit 3D592, and the briefing of the chief of the Supreme Command of the 22nd of April, 1999. That's page 4 in B/C/S and page 4 in the English version. And in item 4, to speed things up, I'll read it while we wait for it. It says, item 4: "The state of war" and "military administration," it's not one and the same thing, military rule, it's not one and the same thing. Could you please explain to us, what does that mean?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume, because I don't see it in front of me, that this is what the chief of Supreme Command Staff said.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Colonel-General Ojdanic, item 4.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it now. And -- despite the fact that this is just a few words, they unequivocally and clearly show the military doctrine of the Army of Yugoslavia, which does not recognise the occupation -- the system of occupation and military rule, which is something that exists under the military doctrine of some other states, including some NATO member states. In the doctrine of the Army of Yugoslavia there is no military rule where the military would suspend the civilian government, would impose some kind of military rule, and would be held responsible for everything that happens in that area. The military engages in armed struggle and it makes sure that other entities involved in the defence, of course, carry out their tasks, but it receives the main brunt.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel and the witness please not overlap.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, we will come back to that and you will provide some other details. You spoke about the control of the territory, General, and the establishment of check-points, does that serve that purpose, too? Can you tell us something about that? Did the military establish those check-points and for what reason, if so?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The corps units did set up check-points at access routes to the sectors where their units were deployed, in order to ensure fuller combat control to prevent any entry of unauthorised persons into the deployment sectors and also to control its own personnel, to prevent them from leaving those sectors.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And what kind of units manned those check-points from the composition of the Pristina Corps?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Primarily those were the units of the military police, because that is their purpose and they have the capability to carry out such tasks. Because they could find themselves in public transport, and one of the roles of the military police is to control the road traffic, military road traffic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, did to that end the security department of the Pristina Corps issue a detailed instruction for the operation of military check-points?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There is a very detailed report, very detailed document on how this task is to be carried out, forms that are to be used for the movement of vehicles, and the security organ actually was in charge of all that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in order to move forward a bit more quickly, the evidence of General Lazarevic on this issue is contained in Exhibit 5D375. There is no reason for us to open this document now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, were there any mixed check-points that were manned both by the military and by the MUP?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As part of the coordinated action in carrying out tasks to establish combat control, we did encounter certain problems, and we agreed in the spirit of cooperation that those check-points should be closer to each other. And each check-point, the police check-point would have its own duties and obligations, and the military check-point would have its own obligations. The military check-point checked military personnel, and the MUP check-points checked their own units and the civilian traffic and all the other civilian structures.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: As far as I was able to understand, those check-points were set up on the basis of an agreement between the leaders of the MUP staff and the Pristina Corps command. Perhaps if we could look at 5D376, and if you could explain to us -- it says here: "Pursuant to an agreement between the leaders of the MUP staff and the Pristina Corps command, the 13th of May," that was the deadline for the resubordination. Is this proof of the fact that the resubordination had not happened by the 13th of May, because we can see from this document that the mixed check-points were set up on the basis of an agreement, that's from the MUP staff leaders?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the document speaks for itself and indicates that this is, indeed, the case. And I just wanted to add that on several occasions, I think it was General Obrad Stevanovic who phoned and tried to get in touch with me in order to have a closer coordinated action with regard to the functioning of those check-points. Perhaps it was also General Lukic, but I remember that I contacted -- I was in contact with General Stevanovic on the phone. So it was done on the basis of an agreement to improve our coordinated action.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now look at exhibit -- a Prosecution exhibit, P1269.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And if you could comment very briefly on items 1 and 5 so that we can proceed more quickly. General, could you please look at this document, the 8th of May, and very briefly items 1 and 5.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an order from the 3rd Army commander from the forward command post about the engagement of the military and MUP forces to establish combat control of the territory. We have been discussing this. In item 1, he orders that all forces should be engaged in the area of responsibility of the corps to establish full control of the territory and the possibility of roads. And in item 5, the Pristina Corps commander, as far as I can see, it was 20 days after the previous order, orders again that the Pristina Corps should resubordinate all military territorial units and the MUP units to the joint units -- tactical units, i.e., brigades.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Just let me see if I understand it correctly. The Pristina Corps commander orders, that's what you said. As far as I can understand from this document, just so that it is clear in the transcript, it was the 3rd Army commander who ordered the Pristina Corps commander on the 8th of May to again issue an order for the resubordination, which had not happened obviously?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, definitely. I do apologise. I may have misspoken, but it is quite clear from this document that this is an order of the 3rd Army commanders to the Pristina Corps commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Let us move on. We've seen that there were some joint actions to rout and destroy Siptar terrorists according to the orders, or rather, the coordinated action between the Army of Yugoslavia, the Pristina Corps, and MUP. Did the units of the Pristina Corps, were they engaged in any independent operations or actions that they carried out on their own?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By your leave, Your Honours, I want to say that the last orders to provide support to the MUP forces with this unfortunate heading of the Joint Command that is now causing this confusion were issued on [as interpreted] the 15th and the 16th of April to carry out counter-insurgency actions. All the other orders, all the other instructions, and all the other combat documents never ever contained this title again. They all pertained to a number of independent actions, battles, and combat engagements of the Pristina Corps within a combat operation, although in some orders the -- there are suggestions or orders for the coordinated action with MUP forces, but in some cases there is no coordinated action. The only units that are engaged are the Pristina Corps units.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: You said up until the 16th, but not after the 16th. Can you explain to us, General, why not after the 16th?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As early as on the 18th, the Supreme Command Staff issued an order for the resubordination of the MUP organs and units to the military, whereby there was no longer any need for any attempts to find some kind of a modality for the coordination and support between the military and MUP; and that is why such headings are no longer seen in any of the corps documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, the English translation says: "On the 15th and 16th of April ..." Was that accurate?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. The General said after the 16th. The General said that the last order with that heading was after the 16th, and my question was: Why after the 16th of April there were no longer any orders bearing this heading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, we will come back to this topic with some documents, but is it true that through -- that this resubordination was attempted until the end of May and did it finally succeed?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd say attempts were made up until the end of the war, and my answer would be that there was no resubordination of the forces, or rather, organs and units of the MUP to the Army of Yugoslavia, quite specifically to the Pristina Corps, as it had been ordered.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, we stopped at the independent actions launched by the Pristina Corps. There is no need to go into the document. I will just make a reference to it, it's 5D335 for the benefit of the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you -- let me ask Mr. Lazarevic: What you're portraying is a picture of persistent attempts to order the resubordination of the MUP forces to the Pristina Corps; is that a correct statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm saying that there were several attempts in addition to the initial order dated the 20th when we're talking about the 3rd Army command, the 20th of April, you saw that on the 8th of May the army commander orders me to resubordinate the MUP units. And on the other hand there were attempts, direct contacts, to do so, but there were problems of another kind. But I have not been asked that question yet so I have refrained from saying that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I was only proceeding on what you said. You said you would say attempts were made up until the end of the war. What were the consequences of the failure of the MUP to accept resubordination?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The consequences, Your Honour, were dire in terms of combat because this resulted in heavy casualties, both in the military ranks and in the MUP ranks because it was impossible to establish heavy combat control in such circumstances, the circumstances of armed rebellion. We suffered heavy casualties, and the defence system in Kosovo and Metohija in certain elements thereof saw its efficiency and effectiveness diminished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm understanding that as saying that these were casualties which might have been avoided had there been resubordination; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is exactly what I'm saying, and if you will bear with me I can tell you in 20 seconds this. Specifically speaking in the Drenica area, the commander of the brigade informed me that some 200 metres from the point of coordinated action a MUP unit was securing that area. There the terrorist units attacked command of the battalion and the commander of the battalion as they were moving and massacred them, him and another five persons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You're painting a picture also of not just the VJ but the MUP suffering additional casualties because of this. Have you any idea why there was a refusal to accept general resubordination?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my information is indirect, not extremely indirect, but it is indirect. I obtained it through the reports of subordinated commanders, through contact with my subordinated army commander, namely, that MUP units in the area of Kosovo and Metohija had not been issued an order from the minister of the interior of the Republic of Serbia to resubordinate themselves to the army units in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija. And they simply could not act upon our orders because the minister of the interior, according to the Law on Internal Affairs is the only authorised person to regulate the use of the operation forces of that ministry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: I just wanted to direct you in regard of these independent actions. The reference is 5D335, 5D361, 3D314, 5D393, and in order not to open them all, we shall just open 5D416, and, General, would you comment on it and then we will move on. General, this appears to be your order, so would you kindly comment on it.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an order seven days prior to the commencement of the second large-scale land operation from Albania of the 19th of May, and I warned the commanders of that fact and I order - let me not say some sort of a partisan tactic - but specifically that all brigades and independent battalions should undertake preparations for the execution of combats, clashes, and all other tactical activities because I assess that there would be a complete severance of the communications and command systems and that the situation in that part of the battle-field would become dramatic. Then I go on to explain how that should be done, and I suggest an order to the commanders, telling them that there would be no assistance from without, but that in keeping with the general order on the defence of the country each one should take their own decisions, in keeping with that general order of mine for the defence of the country.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it is Exhibits 5D393, which are --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: General, I'm sorry to intervene, but this is the right time before we go forward. Could you tell us what were the reasons for the minister of interior not passing orders for resubordination of MUP?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that is a big question mark for me. I don't know whether anyone knows the answer to that in this courtroom. I really don't know why, and I would not like to speculate on that. It was really difficult for me, as was to the other staff of the MUP in Kosovo and Metohija, to comprehend why such orders had not come through, because I had sustained heavy casualties and they had sustained even heavier casualties in the Jablanica region because of the failure to coordinated action. Why that was so, or why that had not been done I really didn't know, I didn't know who Vlajko Stojiljkovic was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: But, sorry, the next question is, General, I'm sorry to ask you this question. Because of the ground realities and the difficult situation you were confronted with, and you also felt the need for cooperation or whatever or working together with the MUP and you wanted that this be formalised, did you agitate this somewhere that why this was not put in a formal way or why formal orders were not being sent or something was not being done? Was there any agitation from your side as the corps commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I certainly did raise in all modesty, let me say, certain activities, and I tried to conduct some sort of a minor mission impossible on my part, and I ordered something which I superiors did not order. You had occasion to see this order of mine, which observed on the strictly military standpoint, I did not have the right to order and interpret things in a way that had not been ordered to me. What I'm trying to tell you is that the kind of order that I received was simply unfeasible in practice; namely, to resubordinate organs and units of the MUP to the corps. What organs? What units? What centres of security? I as the commander did not know what these structures were. Secondly, if you will allow me, let me tell you what I did then. The army commander [as interpreted] who knew all this, but I sent my, so to speak, third man, my assistant, my operations man who I hope will be taking the stand here and we will have occasion to hear him. And he went from secretariat of the interior to secretariat of interior from detachment commander to detachment commander and tried to maintain the necessary level of cooperation. All right. There was no subordination, but we did not want to detract from our mutual relations in order to actually be able to weather this tide of the chaos, war, that we were in the midst of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I certainly don't find that an answer to the question that was asked. Did you agitate with anyone higher up the hierarchy about this? I don't think you've answered that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If, Your Honour, you mean someone from the MUP, from the police --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, no, from your -- anybody who -- I mean, we've seen what General Pavkovic did to try to have this matter raised, but what did you do about it is what Judge Chowhan was asking. No, no, let the witness answer. He's been asked a question and he's been asked whose cage he rattled to try to get something done about this, and he told us he had somebody in the MUP, but Judge Chowhan is more concerned about what he had done through his own chain of command about this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise if I was not sufficiently clear, but I primarily meant my own attitude, my obligation towards the 3rd Army commander, by whom I sat day and night and reported to him, informed him, and I saw and monitored. And you will allow me to say, Your Honour, that that was the utmost I could have done amid that chaos of war. Had I had any other occasion, I would have taken advantage of it, but I was with the commander at all times and I reported on this to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, can I just ask for a minute of your attention. The batch of documents that we have prepared is voluminous and we are trying to follow a system which Your Honours are perhaps unaware of. So that when a subsequent question is raised, and that will be the case, you will actually be able to see what the corps commander and the commander of the army did on that score in their documents, in regards to this question of the resubordination of units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Aleksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honour, I think that page 61, lines 6 and 7, the witness also responded what the 3rd Army commander had taken in connection with that, and it is not reflected in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't understand what you're saying about this. The transcript at present says that he was with the commanders at all times and reported on this to him. What do you say is missing?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, you are asking what measures were taken, and the witness said: I did this and I know that the army commander also took other measures from his competence, and that is not reflected in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I was interrupted twice. I should just like to invoke some exhibits in conjunction with the previous subject matter, that's 5D443 and 5D395.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, did the units of the Pristina Corps suffer frequent attacks by the KLA and did they have significant losses?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not a single day passed in the war without there being losses due to rebel attacks. The losses of the Pristina Corps were twice as high due to terrorist attacks than they were due to NATO attacks.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we refer to 5D221.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: You gave us an example, saying that you ordered the brigades to collect information and plan actions at their own level. Did the command of the Pristina Corps - I'm speaking now of independent actions - did it plan actions at its own level?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For certain situations in the assessment of the corps command, if these situations were serious, the corps command issued special decisions and orders to the brigades, telling them to independently or in cooperation with other brigades carry out these complex tasks in the course of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we now look at Exhibit 5D396.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And could you comment on this, could you tell us whether this is an example of what you were just saying, and especially could you comment on items 4, 5, and 6 on page 2, these are brief. Do you recognise this order?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Please comment on items 4, 5, and 6, this is an order issued by you to break-up and destroy STS in the Kacikol general area.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By Their Honours' leave, let me explain that. In the immediate vicinity of Pristina to the east, some 10 kilometres away, there was a strong build-up of terrorist forces on the main road from Pristina to Medvedja leading to that part of Serbia. I then issued a decision and ordered the 354th Infantry Brigade to become engaged in breaking up this strong build-up which was threatening Pristina itself, and in item 3 I order that they use their own forces for fire support; and as in every other order, I tell them to prevent torching and destroying buildings and to open fire only on buildings where there is resistance and where they pose a danger to their own forces. In item 5, as always, I say prevent maltreatment and persecution of civilians and treat refugees in the spirit of the previously issued orders; in practically every combat order I say this.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: When you say, or rather, you said here open fire only on buildings where there is resistance and where they pose a danger to your own forces. Did the corps carry out an assessment as to how many so-called UBS, that is, lethal weapons, were used in the war and what effects these had?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the meantime let's call up 5D1275.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I beg for Their Honours' indulgence because this appears to be a military question but it is of significance for everything going on in this courtroom. So if Their Honours will bear with me, I will talk about the amount of ordnance used in the war and the amount of ammunition because these facts demonstrate with mathematical accuracy what was done and how. This table was created in the war by counting every bullet and every projectile that was used. This table, however, needs to be seen in the light of what is important here, and that is that the corps did not carry out any kind of systematic campaign of destruction and killing, on the contrary. In my entire military career, I never found another example of this sort of extremely restrictive use of ordnance. If I may, Your Honours, I would like to add a few sentences because it will mean a great deal to me if I can explain with greater precision what this means. According to military doctrine, to carry out a combat task with the minimum of military efficiency, to neutralise 25 per cent of the enemy forces, when this is translated to the situation of the Pristina Corps it would mean that in view of the numbers of rebel forces, the brigades and the zones, as they call them, it would have been necessary to use 0.74 combat kits of the Pristina Corps. The effect of this would have been taking 5 to 6.000 members of the KLA out of action. That would have been the minimum requirement. The second parameter, Your Honours, is that in view of the duration of the war the corps would have had to use 20 combat kits in three months of work. The third parameter contained in the combat documents would be the following: The corps had approval from the 3rd Army to use in the first 15 days of the war four combat kits to carry out its tasks. And finally, in three months of war, the corps used 0.41 per cent of its combat kits. Using this, it could neutralise 10 to 14 per cent of the rebel forces, which is twice less than the minimum. It's half the minimum. According to the combat documentation of the corps, in war with the -- in fighting, 1.095 terrorists were killed, and this amounts to 3 per cent of their numbers, which demonstrates the extreme restrictiveness and use of the principle of humaneness, which was set above the principle of military efficiency. And to conclude, we did this not because we were not well-trained as officers and soldiers, but because had we used bigger and more lethal technology and ordnance, there would have been a lot of destruction and a lot of casualties because the terrorist forces used mainly inhabited places and they used civilians as live shields, human shields. And that was the highest standard of the application of international laws of war and humanitarian laws of war, and there is a whole study that was conducted during and after the war about the use of ordnance and this doctrine of military inefficiency but military humaneness which was set above efficiency. Thank you for bearing with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I hope you understood it, Mr. Bakrac. I find it very difficult to follow any of that, and it's compounded by the fact that the document's not translated. And indeed, I have no idea of the relationship between the document and what's just been said by Mr. Lazarevic. It sounds like an area for expertise if there had been some.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, let me just check the translation. The document has been translated, but I can explain. This is an assessment of the amount of ordnance used, and this was done at the level of the Pristina Corps for the period from the 24th of March to the 10th of May, 1999. General Lazarevic commented on the relationship between the amount of ordnance used and the parameters he explained, which is his view of the situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: When was this document compiled?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 10th of May, 1999, at the command post of the Pristina Corps. This is not an assessment, Your Honours, it's a report of the rear organ on the use of ammunition up to the 10th of May, 1999, and there are other reports for the period up to the end of the war. This document refers to the numbers of projectiles and the numbers of bullets used by the units of the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we may return to it later once I've seen the translation, but I can make nothing of it as it stands. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. We have information that there is a translation, and during the break we will try to discover why it is not on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, we said that the civil authorities continued functioning in Kosovo and Metohija. What tasks were they performing inter alia?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to the best of my knowledge, which is indirect and which I obtained through the officers subordinate to me because I have to say I did not have any direct contacts except perhaps an exchange of letters within individuals, but I really do know from the reports coming from my subordinate units that they exerted enormous efforts to take care of the civilian population, to make sure that public services continued to function, that the population was supplied with necessities, and that after strikes, everything would continue to function, the market inspection, the judiciary, everything that's needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, to avoid looking at each and every document and to expedite matters, I'll just give you the references, 2D375, 5D29, 5D1199.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, we touched on this issue a little while ago, so let's round it off now. The question relates to the relationship between the civilian authorities and particular units which were part of the army and of the 3rd Corps. In the case of the Army of Yugoslavia, were there any misunderstandings of the role of the Army of Yugoslavia in wartime and its relationship with the structures of the civilian authorities and the civilian government, because we saw that a state of war implies military administration. So could you comment on this and then we'll look at a Prosecution document.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I learned about several such occurrences here in this courtroom. In that period during the time of the war, I did not have information that any units of the army acted incorrectly or undertook things that were not within their competence, but I learned about this here.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Please look at P1208. This refers to the command of the Pec Military District. The commander of the Pec Military District issued an order on the 30th of May, 19 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: -- 30th of March, 1999. Could you please comment on item 1 and then we'll move on and round off this topic before the break.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commander of the Pec Military District, which was part of the Pristina Military District and subordinated to the 3rd Army at the time, on the 30th of March, 1999, referring to a non-existent order by the supreme commander ordered that all republican and other local authorities be placed under the command of the Pec military district. My comment on this is that it just doesn't make sense, that it's absolute nonsense. There's nothing one can say about such a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Now look at 5D37, please, dated the 25th of April, 1999, and please comment on it. It's a brief document.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The very same commander that issued the nonsensical order that we have just seen cancelled, revoked, his previous order on the 25th of April that was based on the military -- Pristina Military District command, and I know for a fact that the commander of the Pristina Military District under my command used my previous order in which I prohibited the issuing of any orders related to the civilian government and used it as a basis to revoke his own document.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at P -- Exhibit P1982, again a Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: If you could comment on that, if you know what that is.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is yet another similar document, this time it is the 7th Infantry Brigade that had just a few days before that arrived. It was transferred to the Pristina Corps area. Again he refers to this non-existent order, but in milder terms establishes some kind of staffs, Municipal Assemblies, coordinates orders. This is couched in different terms, determining who would take care of the civilians, protect law and order, but it is without a shadow of a doubt an order that cannot be carried out by anyone, including the addressees, and nobody has the right to issue such an order. And when the order -- when he received the order on the 23rd of March [as interpreted], he for all intents and purposes revoked this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: The order that we're referring to now, we've already called it up, that's 5D374, this is an order of the Pristina Corps commander of the 23rd of April prohibiting in item 5 any such actions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I apologise, but there is an error in the transcript, it's not March -- yes, yes, it's my mistake. It's the 23rd of March. In fact, when I gave the reference -- no, I'm sorry. Let's clear this up.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: This order of yours, what date does it bear?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 23rd of April, as far as I can remember, measures to stabilize the defence. That's what it is called.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Yes, well there was an error in the transcript, so now we've clarified it. Did the military district command, following this order of yours, the Pristina Military District command issue its own order? Because we saw that the units within its composition had tried to do something like that. That would be 5D35, Exhibit 5D35, we can look at it on the screen, in particular item 4, 5D35. Page 2, item 4. That is when the Pristina Military District command was resubordinated to you.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, resubordinated, he is quoting my order, I prohibit any issuing on any orders on this part of the commanders regarding the functioning of the Crisis Staffs or authorities, and all the other commands complied with my order.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps this would be a convenient time for a break. I think, according to our schedule, we should have our break now for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We shall resume at 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, we talked about the relationship between the Army of Yugoslavia and the civilian authorities. You touched upon the relationship with the MUP. Maybe we with wrap up this topic. Let me ask you the following: What was the relationship between the Army of Yugoslavia, the corps units, and the MUP units during the war and in what way was the coordination done and at what level?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say that the relations were correct in accordance with the purpose and function of those two structures within the defence system. As for the coordination, it was carried out in accordance with the instruction and the Rules of Combat of Army of Yugoslavia. As for the level, during the war the coordination at the higher level, the MUP staff and the corps command, was practically impossible because of constant relocations and constant engagements. And it boiled down to individual contacts between the people from the corps command and people either in the staff or outside of the staff, Brakovic, General Stefanovic, who was a colonel in the -- and Stefanovic, who was the colonel in the corps command, and it was going on to a much higher extent at the level of the brigade commanders and the secretariats of the interior and the commanders of those.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please speak into the microphone. The interpreters couldn't hear the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We heard -- there are no documents from the staff command or the corps command that does not regulate the coordination. It is something that must be done in combat conditions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Was there a Stevanovic both in the VJ and in the MUP?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I want to cut a long story short and then I'm inconsistent. One of the assistants in the MUP, the assistant to the minister of the interior was General Obrad Stevanovic. And in the Pristina Corps command there was the colonel, Radojko Stefanovic, he was the chief of the operations and training organ. So there's just one sound that distinguishes the two surnames, but they dealt with the coordination, so did Colonel Brakovic from the police. This is as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, lest we should be opening all those documents, 5D997, 5D333, and 5D369 all speak about this relationship.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, now I would like to ask you - and this is something that we started talking about before the break - the issue of resubordination. This is something that has been discussed at length in this courtroom. You said that there had been no resubordination.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please now look at --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: We've seen often here in courtroom an order from the supreme commander and the Chief of the General Staff and the army commander, that's 4D299. Now I would like us to see 51267 [as interpreted]. It's your document, it's dated the 20th of April, if we could elicit your comments?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Could you give us that number again, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's P1267, it's a Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: It appears to be your order, and His Honour Judge Chowhan, if I understood it correctly, he asked you if you had issued any orders. So this is the order for the resubordination dated the 20th of April. Could you please comment on it. You said something that it contains more items than the previous ones.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By the Trial Chamber's leave I would like to say that resubordination as a process, as an action, is something that is extremely complex. And if I may be allowed to say that we've heard in this courtroom some comments ranging from a statement that it was impossible to resubordinate to such institutions. We heard that from a general that had been doing that for 30 years in the military and all the way up to a statement that this is something that can be done ad hoc, in two, three hours. And I assure you, based on my personal experience, it is mission impossible, I use that term for the second or third time today. Acting on the orders of the 3rd Army commander, referring to the order of the Supreme Command Staff, on the 20th of April I issued an order. In item 1 I copy the two referenced orders and, Your Honour, let me read what it says here so that we all get an idea of how difficult it is. "Units and organs of the Ministry of the Interior of Serbia, in the brigades' zones of responsibility shall be resubordinated to the brigade commands for carrying out combat tasks." There are two departments here. No units, no organs, I assure you, for me this was simply impossible to carry out, to implement; and that is why I was late in drafting this order. And to be quite frank, I have to tell you that I also wrote an order that contained only two or three sentences, and then I tore them up and then I tried to draft something really smart. I tried to say that the MUP units, without enumerating which units, should continue carrying out their regular tasks in terms of protecting the personal and -- security of person and property and the law and order, and that in terms of combat they should be resubordinated to the brigades. And I even came up with this deadline, I invented this deadline, because I was -- I could see that this was not easy to do. So this is the gist of this order that I sent to my subordinate units, and I think that you can see that this was also sent to the MUP staff in Pristina, it's down there at the edge of this sheet. You can't see it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, who was your opposite number in the MUP in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would like to know that after all these years. I stand here in front of you as an accused and yet I don't know that. In the military you know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Did you try to identify who that was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To this date I don't know that. It hasn't been defined. In the military you know that the lower-ranked units are resubordinated to the higher-ranked units. It is impossible for an assistant minister of the interior to be resubordinated to me or an organ that was established by the minister to be resubordinated to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We've had some evidence, though, that what you needed to do at a lower level in trying to arrange resubordination was to persuade the appropriate MUP official or officer to make an order that his unit was to be resubordinated to you. Now, it sounds as though you didn't make any effort to liaise with someone at your level in the MUP to try to achieve that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With all due respect of all the "experts," including one that we heard here, whoever discusses resubordination in those terms, in the military sense, does not know what resubordination is. Let me be quite specific. I ordered at the beginning of the war that the units of the Pristina Corps should comply with the Rules of Service of the Army of Yugoslavia in wartime, the rules on military discipline. How can a member of the police comply with the Rules of Service of the Army of Yugoslavia when he does not belong to the Army of Yugoslavia, he's not a member? So who was I to search for in Kosovo and Metohija and to tell him, Well, you are my opposite number. In the army you issue an order, an order is obeyed. I was not given an order as to who was being resubordinated to me. The Defence counsel quoted from both orders, he referred to both those orders in a couple of sentences, and on the basis of that it was impossible to carry out that task. It is impossible to do it on the basis of this order here. This was just an effort to blend together oil and water, as we say. It is impossible to do so. We heard this man from the General Staff who testified in this case that it was, indeed, impossible. An order was written. I did it, I acted accordingly, but that mission failed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Who is the person from the General Staff to whom you're referring?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Kosovac, the man who had been dealing with organization at the level of General Staff in the military for 30 years, and I think that he is one of the biggest experts on this particular issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You began your answer by saying "with all due respect to all the experts, including one in particular, who was the expert in particular that you were referring to at that stage?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Actually, I meant to correct myself, Your Honour, when I referred to experts, I meant those who perhaps had aspirations after expertise, and I said there was just one expert who we saw here but that did not refer to him. In a way I wanted to say that what we heard in this courtroom with my knowledge of the facts, not to mention military doctrine, that is simply not possible the way it has been described by some.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just deal with my question. The English translation of the start of your answer suggests to me that you were being critical of Mr. Radinovic. Would that be a mistake on my part, to understand your evidence that way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With due respect, I didn't misspeak. What I did say was that one expert was here. I did not comment on his positions on resubordination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, did you get reports from subordinated units on abortive attempts at resubordination?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the meantime we can call up on the screen Exhibit 5D792.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: One separate question, Mr. Lazarevic. Assume for the moment that the order made by the Supreme Command Staff for resubordination had, in fact, been communicated to the appropriate person in the MUP, assume that for the moment, are you saying that even then, in these circumstances, resubordination just cannot be made to work properly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am convinced of that and I answer-- my answer to your hypothesis is affirmative because these are two systems of responsibility of control and command of organization of functioning. And from what I know from the military aspect of what resubordination is, it cannot refer to these two systems. Your Honour, you cannot ad hoc resubordinate and end the story there. Resubordination implies commanding the formation in question. Prior to the execution of a task, a task has to be received. There should be preparations. The task should run its course, and action can be for three days, but combat control and the defence of the state lasted for three months.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, I'm going to repeat my question and we already have PD792 [as interpreted] on the screen in front of us. Did you receive from subordinated units reports about failed resubordination exercises? You can take a look at this supplementary combat report of the 23rd of April, 1999, and at the very bottom of the page it is written: "Units -- MUP units from Istok."

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Specifically starting on the 20 of April, the first day of readiness, to put it that way, up to the 10th of June, units reported on failure to execute that task, some in harsher form, others in less harsh form. Here specifically we have the report of the 7th Motorised Brigade of the 25th of April, where they report that units of the MUP from Istok and Klina, despite our request, have not do this date submitted to us any figures, any data, on their available sources and resources, but are awaiting a decision of the superiors on resubordination to our brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And that is the 7th Infantry Brigade. General, when I stop I'm actually waiting for the translation to end, for the interpretation to end. So this is the interim combat report of the 23rd. Let us now look at 5D795 of the 25th of -- your deadline for resubordination. So the exhibit number is 5D795.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see page 3 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Take a look at the penultimate or the two penultimate paragraphs, rather.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is the last page in the English version as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The commander of the brigade is informing me that pursuant to my order of the 20th of April, resubordination of MUP units in Klina and Istok was to be carried out to the brigade. By the order of the brigade of the 21st of April, the same were under the obligation to submit reports by the 23rd on their available forces and resources. The same have not done so, avoid cooperation with our unit, stating that they are waiting for a decision from their superior organs. Please take measures at your level for the implementation of this order.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did you send to the brigades operations organs from the corps to see what the problem was? And later in May, on the 17th of May --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see 5D1084.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a combat report of the commander of the 37th Motorised Brigade from the 17th of May, 1999, informing me that Colonel Stefanovic, the one whom I mentioned, at Paprica from the corps command were visiting the unit in connection with the resubordination of territorial police units in the brigade's area of responsibility. So I personally sent teams from the corps command to the brigades. I dispatched to look for command -- police commanding officers on the ground to coordinate with them. And if they couldn't do so, my order, my request, was that they should maintain cooperation on the level of - shall I put it this way - combat feasibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Exhibit 5D817 is along the same lines in order for us to proceed expeditiously. General, did you report -- did you inform the superior command on the failure to resubordinate; and if so, when?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometime between the 20th and the 23rd of April I had several repeated reminders from the commander of the 37th Motorised Brigade to the effect that he had -- he was encountering problems regarding resubordination, that he had increased casualties. He referred to the Travnik [as interpreted] incident with five people being massacred from the battalion command, to which I reacted by saying to the -- by saying in written form to the army commander, although we were together at the same command post every day, that there was no resubordination conducted in keeping with his order. This is not that document on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, 79, 24, it's not Travnik, it's tragic accident.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have Prosecution Exhibit P179 -- 23.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Can you take a look at it and tell us whether it is your document on the -- on failure to resubordinate --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can we have the number again, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P1723.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, this is a document of the corps commander sent personally to the commander of the 3rd Army, in which attention is drawn to the fact that according to the order of the army commander there was no resubordination of the MUP forces, notwithstanding a number of -- of -- despite a number of meetings having been held to discuss that particular issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, I can see here that you indicated that there were problems and unresolved questions, in view of the fact that the MUP was tolerating criminal activities on the part of its members. Can you explain? On what basis did you say that?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We spoke today about the work of mixed check-points, and this sentence, this statement, refers to reports by primarily the 37th Motorised Brigade, to the effect that the work of the mixed check-points was fraught with numerous problems and unresolved questions. And as the commander of brigade suggests -- or actually, he is informing me that allegedly the MUP was tolerating criminal activities by its members. Appraising the possible gravity of that piece of information, I informed the army commander of it in written form.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if you will bear with me for just one minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, can we have Exhibit 5D376 brought up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: This is dated the 13th of May. It is a letter by the staff leader.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see the second page.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: You told us that this is associated with the check-points. Did you have this piece of information, that the leader of the MUP staff requested that all measures be taken at the check-points in order to improve the conduct and the appearance of the police there? Is this what you had in mind when you said what you did? Please take a look at the final, last, paragraph.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a document by the staff leader -- staff head of the MUP, General Lukic. I believe that pursuant to the information that he had available -- made available to him by my people, and also from a mutual exchange of information with people from the military - and I mean primarily the security organs - that he took measures and that this possibly also refers to such occurrences. Concretely I haven't seen this particular document during the war, but I'm quite confident because I know that whatever information we received from the MUP we took it into very serious consideration and checked it, either on our own or with them. But -- and we took joint measures with MUP organs in order to ascertain the truth. And with the permission of the Trial Chamber I should just like to add one sentence, namely, that in that war there were numerous or quite a few, shall I say, instances of reporting that did not correspond to the reality, to the truth, coming from various quarters. The commander of the army was very zealous, and he demanded that everything be addressed and resolved in a very short procedure as urgently as possible. I have to say so even though he is present here. He had commissions set up, and that indeed yielded results. I personally insisted that whenever any information was obtained, that every effort should be exerted for the truth to be ascertained. Let me not give you any further examples. I just want to tell you how seriously we took all this information, how in earnest we checked it and verified it, whether it came from subordinated or any other entities. Sometimes I didn't know from whom they came. The commander of the army would be by me, and, for instance, we heard that the army went inside a depot near Pristina and took some technical goods from there. And I would say, General, that is impossible, allow me, give me three hours to check that out. He didn't allow me. He set up a commission himself, and it was ascertained that it had not been the military, but it had been some civilians who did that. I apologise for having spoken at such length. I just wanted to give you a concrete example of such practices.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, we saw here - and we also have Exhibit 5D434 to show it, and it is a report on a tour by the staff of the Supreme Command, the tour was carried out from the 23rd to the 26th of May, 1999. And on the 24th, you wrote this information that there had not been resubordination.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have this document on the screen, page 4, item 11.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And could you please comment on it. It's a report of the team of the Supreme Command Staff. Page 4, item 11. In this report in item 11, does it say that resubordination had failed to take place?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This team from the General Staff wrote in this report that there was no single command for forces, no unified command, but that cooperation with MUP units is achieved through agreements which are not respected at lower levels. Although cooperation is functioning for the present, should there be an escalation of the aggression this could have serious consequences for the members of the MUP and the army. And there is no doubt that this team also observed and noted this fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. And to round off this topic --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I would like now to have 5D1289 called up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: This is a document issued by the Ministry of the Interior, and the last paragraph - it's dated the 6th of May, this whole document, 1999 - and this last paragraph, is it also evidence that resubordination had failed to take place and who was responsible for the MUP units?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the document speaks for itself --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Just a minute, General. I do apologise for interrupting you. I thought that we would not have a problem with translation. Most documents have been translated, but this translation has not arrived yet. So could you please read the document very slowly. We'll have it marked for identification. The last paragraph is very brief. Could you read it out slowly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, the translation -- we have the translation in e-court, but it would take me a second to find the number, but we do have it. If you want me to spend a little bit of time, I can find it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It would be helpful if you do so but I think Mr. Bakrac just wishes the last paragraph read, and we can proceed with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would indicate that 5D434 is -- this exhibit appears to be the duplicate of one that's already in evidence, that's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's what Mr. Ackerman said.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, I believe it's 3D692, and it was in evidence on the 12th of September.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I do apologise. Errors do occur. Our documents seem to have got mixed up. There's a large number of documents. If 3D will make it easier for us to follow, then I would like to ask for 3D692 to be called up on the screen. No, Your Honour, that's not it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let's go back to your exhibit and ask the witness to do what you asked him already, read the last paragraph. Mr. Visnjic. Hold on, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, just let me say the following. Mr. Hannis referred to the 3D number which is the same as 5D454, the previous document used by Mr. Bakrac, not the last one that was in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have 5D1289.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And then please read that sentence, it's very brief, so we can move on.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "For the situation on the ground, the behaviour and work of members of the MUP and the carrying out of the instructions given, the following shall be responsible: "The heads of the secretariats and the commanders of PJP detachments and SAJ detachments, those are the special anti-terrorist units."

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, I have an objection about the last one. We don't have a translation. There appears to be a signature but I don't see a stamp on it so I have a concern about the authenticity, and it's particularly a problem when I can't read the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, what is this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this document is from the ministry headquarters in Pristina. It's not a military document.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if you look at this document you will see that it has the stamp, or rather, the ERN number of the Prosecution Y0048073. It's from the EDS, so the Prosecutor should take care of the authenticity of his own documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: He's perhaps decided that he's so doubtful of its authenticity that he hasn't used it for all we know, Mr. Bakrac. Mr. Hannis, are you still concerned about its authenticity?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I am, Your Honour. I'm checking -- I understand most of these with the ERN that start with the Y are documents that we received from Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, let me return to what I was asking. Have you seen this document before this trial?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, what's the point you're trying to make with this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my client is charged in the indictment of having effective control and command over forces which are listed, and they include forces of the MUP and PJP; however, here we have a document showing who was issuing orders and who was in control and it's a document dated the 6th of May. Therefore, I feel it's a very significant document for our defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, you'll need to do some work on establishing the authenticity of this document. We will not allow it to be exhibited in -- without some substantiation, such as confirmation of who was responsible for it. That need not be by method of a stamp, but you will need to find some way of authenticating it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, in view of the fact, as we have heard that there was no resubordination, how did the cooperation between the Army of Yugoslavia and the Ministry of the Interior proceed?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say that this cooperation continued at the same level as before, with mutual respect and attempts to survive the horrors of war. And by Their Honours' leave, the end of the war was dramatic. A whole basic MUP unit found itself in a very difficult situation in the Jablanica area. They were completely surrounded, and I ordered a combat operation to rescue that unit. There were losses in the army in that action. So what I want to say is that the obligation to defend the country and to carry out our tasks was always respected, and what we could not do was impossible. I'm not trying to justify either myself or General Lukic, but truly I'm telling you that as direct participants we did our very best to carry out these tasks under the prevailing conditions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the reference for the continuation of cooperation is 5D444 and 5D448.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And my last question on this topic: You mentioned carrying out a deblockade of the MUP forces surrounded by terrorists. When was this in Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was in late May, as far as I can recall, and there were heavy losses. There was danger that the entire unit would be decimated. I issued an order that the whole action - and that's what it was called, the action for deblocking the MUP units, it's a rather odd title, but that was the name of the combat action.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Excuse me, just a moment. Your Honour, just for the record, that document 5D376 is actually in e-court with Prosecution Exhibit Number P2159, and so the translation is available there. So it is a Prosecution exhibit but not admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that's where it shall remain for the moment. Thank you, Mr. Ackerman. Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I ask for your guidance. It's not exhibited, but it was used by the Prosecutor so is it up to me to establish its authenticity?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's not being suggested it was used by the Prosecutor. It simply is in his system as one of his potential exhibits. Now that you wish to use it, you require to establish its authenticity.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I misunderstood the interpretation. I thought that they had used it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, did the command of the Pristina Corps take any measures to assist the civilian population and the civilian authorities in looking after the civilian population? And while you are responding, I will ask for Exhibit P1306, a Prosecution exhibit, to be called up on the screen. It was not used by the Prosecution, but my colleague Mr. Hannis promised me that he would not object to its being used. This was in April 2007, if my learned friend recalls. So it's P1306, the command of the Pristina Corps, it's dated the 16th of April, 1999, securing the civilian population to the commander personally. It seems to be your document. It seems that you not only signed it but also drafted it, General. Can you comment on it for us? I think this order is important, so please go slowly item by item.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's no doubt about the authenticity of this document. I composed it under difficult circumstances, and I confess that I tried to do something that was not strictly in line with military rules and military doctrine. And now as an accused, I have tried to find an example of something like this in military science, but I haven't found anything. This was just an attempt that I made to establish within the corps units special elements of combat which would secure the civilian population from accommodation, looking after them in all respects, supplies, helping to shelter them, assisting, providing supplies, organizing economic activities, medical support, and so on and so forth. This is a permanent order. All units had to establish special forces which would deal with assisting the civilian population. I required that all members of the corps be familiarised with this order and that they consistently carry it out, that all commanders carry it out consistently and brief me on its implementation. That is the essence of one such order in conditions where I myself couldn't know how many of my soldiers were killed or wounded every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Let us now move on to Exhibit 5D389. I would like you to look at it and to comment on it briefly.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an order which serves to operationalise further the previous order, in the sense that the brigade commanders are required with the assistance of the civil authorities to find safe sectors, facilities, and premises to house the civilian population and to tell me where there were such facilities, such buildings, that were not under threat of combat operations and were not constantly targeted by NATO air-strikes.
